Hatchlings of Arctic char emerge from the gravel redd at a total length of approximately 2 centimeters [Lb = approximately 2 centimeters], a diminutive size that constrains their early foraging capacity and vulnerability to predation. Embryonic development proceeds over a period of 44 days  when eggs are incubated at a stable thermal regime of 8.5 °C [T = 8.5 °C], a duration that aligns closely with the 39 to 49 day range reported for other cold-water salmonids. Once emerged, the alevins remain dependent on their yolk reserves during an endotrophic phase, and the interval from egg deposition to the moment of hatching eclosion, when the chorion is ruptured, encompasses roughly 44 days under those controlled conditions. The brief period of yolk-sac resorption is soon followed by the onset of exogenous feeding as the mouth opens and first prey capture occurs, marking the transition from lecithotrophic to exotrophic nutrition. During these earliest life stages, the larvae are particularly sensitive to thermal variation; deviations from the optimal 8.5 °C incubation temperature can accelerate or delay the timing of hatching enzyme activation and thus shift the entire phenology of emergence.

Reproductive investment in Arctic char is governed by the size at which females first attain sexual maturity, a milestone that corresponds to a total length of 35 centimeters [Lp = 35 centimeters]. Individuals that have not yet reached this somatic threshold do not initiate gonadal recrudescence and instead divert resources toward continued somatic growth. Once this length is achieved, the onset of vitellogenesis and spermiation becomes possible, though the exact timing of first reproduction depends on local environmental conditions such as food availability and thermal history. Under the thermal conditions typical of this species' spawning environment (7 °C [T = 7 °C]), the maximum reproductive rate has been estimated from field-based observations; a gravid female may produce approximately 3000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 3000 eggs per spawning event], with around one spawning event occurring per year [F_R_i = around one spawning event occurring per year], a figure reflecting the protracted reproductive cycle characteristic of high-latitude salmonids. This value represents the upper limit of reproductive effort under favorable feeding regimes, though in practice many females skip spawning in years of poor condition. The iteroparous life history of this species means that reproductive output is distributed across multiple seasons, and the total lifetime egg production is shaped by the interplay between body size, age, and the prevailing thermal environment of the lake or river system.

The ultimate body dimensions achieved by Arctic char in productive lake systems are considerable, with the maximum recorded total length reaching 107 centimeters [Li = 107 centimeters] and the corresponding ultimate wet weight attaining 15,000 grams [Wwi = 15,000 grams]. These values characterize the largest individuals observed in long-term monitoring programs, typically old females that have accumulated somatic tissue over many growing seasons. The wet weight at hatch, by contrast, is a mere 0.0044 grams , a mass so modest that it underscores the enormous magnitude of postnatal growth spanning nearly seven orders of magnitude from the alevin stage to the spawning adult. This prodigious increase in body mass requires a prolonged juvenile phase dedicated to feeding and growth before the energy reserves necessary for reproduction can be accumulated. Comparisons with congeneric species such as Salvelinus fontinalis reveal that Arctic char exhibit a somewhat greater asymptotic size, likely an adaptation to the deep, oligotrophic lakes they often inhabit where prey resources are patchy but large-bodied individuals can exploit a wider trophic niche. The allometric shifts that accompany this growth trajectory involve changes in fin ray ossification and body plan reorganization during the larval-juvenile transition, after which the fingerlings begin to exhibit the characteristic color pattern of the species.

Longevity in Arctic char is strongly modulated by temperature, with the maximum lifespan reaching 4 years [am = 4 years] when fish are maintained at a mean annual water temperature of 5 °C [T = 5 °C]. This relatively short lifespan for a salmonid of its body size reflects the metabolic costs imposed by the cold, unproductive environments this species typically occupies; in warmer lakes or in captive rearing conditions, lifespan may be extended due to slower growth rates and reduced metabolic demands. The age at which exogenous feeding begins, which is equivalent to the age at birth from the perspective of independent nutrition, has been determined under controlled conditions at 7 °C [T = 7 °C] to be approximately 70.5 days [ab = approximately 70.5 days]. Following this transition to active foraging, the young-of-year enter a period of rapid mass gain during the first summer, when prey densities are highest and day length is maximal at high latitudes. The natural mortality rate is highest during the first winter, when the juveniles must contend with ice cover, reduced prey availability, and the energetic challenge of meeting their daily energy needs under low temperatures.

The age at which Arctic char first spawns has been determined from mark-recapture studies in Subarctic lakes, with individuals initiating reproductive activity at 3 years after hatching [tR = 3 years after hatching] when the lake system experiences a mean summer temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. This timing of first reproduction is tightly linked to the attainment of the 35 centimeter [Lp = 35 centimeter] total length at puberty, and in slower-growing populations, the age at first spawning may be delayed to 4 or even 5 years. The spawning migration typically occurs in late summer, with adults moving from deeper feeding areas toward gravel-bottomed littoral zones where females excavate redds. The total length at puberty, at which point the HPG axis is activated and gonadal recrudescence begins, represents a critical threshold in the life history; individuals that have reached this length are capable of participating in the annual spawning event, though not all do so each year. The energy allocated to gamete production is substantial, and females that have spawned often exhibit depleted lipid stores and reduced body condition in the following spring. This trade-off between current reproduction and future survival is a defining feature of the iteroparous strategy, limiting the maximum lifespan to approximately 4 years in many populations.
